title: AI Is Coming for Tasks Before It Comes for Jobs
summary: Neil Thompson on What Workers Actually Think, Why Big Firms Win, and Where the Human Still Fits. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . MIT FutureTech director Neil Thompson joins Ben Lorica to discuss how AI is reshaping work, the economy, and the future of automation. Drawing on recent research, Thompson explains why AI’s impact on most occupations may unfold gradually rather than arrive as a sudden shock, why adoption continues to lag behind technical capabilities, and why the fixed costs of implementation favor larger firms. They also explore the future of entry-level jobs and professional training, the changing economics of consulting, emerging AI safety risks, and whether open-weight models will eventually dominate inference. Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter Interview highlights – key sections from the video version: Introduction to Neil Thompson and MIT FutureTech Revisiting the Computational Limits of Deep Learning: Scaling Costs and Algorithmic Progress Beyond Chatbots: Jev, Task Routing, and More Efficient AI Systems Beyond Traditional Benchmarks: Measuring AI’s Real-World Impact Inside the Crashing Waves vs. Rising Tides Study: Methodology and Worker Evaluations Crashing Waves vs. Rising Tides: How AI Automation Spreads Across Jobs Measuring Complex Tasks: Using Human Task Duration as a Proxy AI and Mathematics: Verification, Human Expertise, and Quality Gaps The Apprenticeship Dilemma: What Happens When AI Replaces Entry-Level Tasks? Why AI Adoption Lags Behind Technical Capabilities The Productivity Bottleneck: Why More AI-Generated Code Doesn’t Mean More Software Releases The Economics of AI Automation: Fixed Costs, Scale, and the Advantage of Large Firms Which Industries Will Lead AI Adoption, and How Will Consulting Change? AI Safety Risks: Cybersecurity, Biological Threats, and Catastrophic Outcomes Open vs. Closed Models: The Future of Inference, Distillation, and Competition Jump to transcript Related content : A video version of this conversation is available on our YouTube channel . Neil Thompson → The Computational Limits of Deep Learning Crashing Waves vs. Rising Tides: Findings on AI Automation from Thousands of Worker Evaluations of Labor Market Task AI, Scale, and Task-Based Theories of Automation Richard Ho → Inside OpenAI’s First Chip Ben Lorica and Evangelos Simoudis → Navier-Stokes and AI generated work: If You Can’t Explain It, Did You Really Do It? How AI Is Changing Mathematical Research Support our work by subscribing to our newsletter Transcript Below is a polished and edited transcript . Ben Lorica. All right. So today we welcome back Neil Thompson, director of MIT’s FutureTech Research Project, who was last on the podcast in the year of COVID, October 2020. So Neil, welcome back to the podcast. Neil Thompson. It’s my pleasure to be here. Ben Lorica. So I guess before we start, give us a one sentence, one to two sentence description of the future tech project. Neil Thompson. Yeah, so we are a we’re a research group that is sits both within the computer science AI Lab and the Sloan School of Management, both at MIT, were one of MIT’s largest research groups. We got more than 100 people, and we’re quite unusual in that we’re about half computer scientists and half economists. And so we try and think both about technically what’s going on and how you can put that into big models so that we know how it’s going to affect people, how it’s going to change growth, those kind of big questions, and at some some deeper level, you know, if we think broadly about the things we do, we think about what’s driving AI progress, what effects it’s going to have, and then we also do some work specifically on AI risk, which, as you can imagine, has been a lot in the last week or so. Ben Lorica. Yeah, yeah. All right. So the reason I have Neil back is they have a couple of really interesting papers that caught my eye. But when Neil was last here, we talked about a paper they released at the time on the computational limits of deep learning . So maybe let’s go quickly and score that paper . I guess six years after the fact, so I guess one of the things that it got right early was the cost pressure, right? So around chips, capital, electricity, things like that, right? So let’s let’s stay on the positive side of the ledger, first. So, what are the things you feel that paper got right? Neil Thompson. Yeah. So, I think what you said is right. I think we were we were on the right side of it in terms of saying like this seems like one that the scaling laws are one of the main drivers, and I think indeed that you know has has been true, and that meant that we were going to progress from systems that were really not that expensive to systems that were very expensive, and where that cost pressure was going to be important. And of course, now we’re really seeing that, right? We see these systems where all of a sudden people are like, “Ah, maybe don’t use the most advanced system for these things. So I think that’s one of the things we got right. I think another thing we got right, but didn’t call enough, is when we actually did the economic modeling of this, we implicitly put in some terms for algorithmic progress, right? And we were people were really not talking about algorithmic progress in that we sort of we had had measured in that, but we really didn’t know sort of what was going on there. We really didn’t call it out very much, and I think it was just stuff that we people in Epoch and a few other places did over these the coming years to say, oh, let’s actually call that out and realize how important that is. So I think those were sort of the two things that we got right. I also have one big thing we got wrong, which if you want to make that turn yet,. Ben Lorica. Yeah. So on the on the algorithmic on the algorithmic progress, I guess you folks kind of hinted at it at a high level, as you mentioned. But obviously, on the specifics, like you know, now we’re using mixture of experts, maybe quantization, distillation, and so on, right? So, but at least you kind of hinted that’s probably going to happen just because of pressure. Neil Thompson. Yeah. So, so we I mean we knew that algorithmic progress was going to happen you know had to happen. Like we said that pressure was there, but we actually implicitly, if you actually look at the regressions we ran where we were trying to estimate how fast these models were improving, we put in effects that said over time you might be able to get more out of it, and so we were actually implicitly already measuring that. But as I say, like the problem was we didn’t know exactly what was the thing that was going on there, so we didn’t really call it out at that point. But what’s clear is you can even go back to that thing and you can see that it’s actually a very substantial number, and so this is you know I think that’s turned out to be something you know you gave a couple of examples of it of course by far the biggest example was transformers when they came out but those are the kind of things where you’ve seen suddenly we can harness every additional you know GPU much more effectively that’s made a big difference and particularly made a big difference for the biggest models that people use. Ben Lorica. Yeah and so there were there was there were a lot of innovations or or at least adjustments on the algorithm side, but also just on serving and inference, right? So speculative decoding and things like this, right? So, but. That came that came after the fact when obviously there was much more heavy usage, right? Neil Thompson. Exactly, right. I mean, there has been a lot of pressure. I mean, I think you know we correctly called out that pressure, although at least I was surprised by the extent to which I wish people had been able to do it, right? The amount that they’ve been able to get year after year in things like making inference more efficient, right, has been remarkable. More so than I imagined at the time. At the time we thought that people were going to move more towards traditional algorithms. So we know that at some very deep level, AI like the deep learning algorithm is actually pretty inefficient way to learn things, and we thought that people would push it towards sort of more like base level algorithms where we know they’re optimal for the problem, and we really have not seen that. Right, the ability to do that training all at once has been so powerful that it’s only in this last little bit as we’ve gotten into agentic systems, where now suddenly we still have the AI doing it, but now it’s calling a tool, and that tool, of course, can have a very efficient way of doing something. So it, you know, calls a C library that sorts a list or something like that, and it doesn’t actually have to sort that list itself. And so we sort of we sort of finally got into it, but we were imagining that would be more of a heart of how AI was trained, and now it’s really more like AI has just been trained in a very broad way, and now we have it learning to use tools, and they can now learn to use those tools efficiently. Ben Lorica. And of course, we’re recording this on the week when the biggest new, or one of the biggest news among developers, is the release of this, or the announcement of a project called Jev, which I don’t know if you’ve been following this thing. It’s a, it’s a, it’s kind of gotten a lot of attention. But basically, at a high level, you know, it’s just that realization of going back to basics, right? So, which is, do you really need a chatbot for everything, right? So, in other words, what these systems like and by the way Jev turns out to be built on ideas from even Bert and people have built systems similar to Jev. But what Jev does is basically okay. So what are you asking? All right. So I’m gonna decide and route to the right thing. Right. So it’s it’s more than a router in some ways. So it’s it’s basically I guess a good example is you know if you’re in DevOps, right? So our site has been down for two hours and we are losing money. Fix this now. So an LLM will say, yeah, it looks like the site is down. I would route this to the infrastructure team, right? So, whereas models like Jev would go, okay, so what’s the what’s the probability that we should route this to the infrastructure team? Score it, right? So, at what level of urgency? Score it, right? So what is this going to cost churn? Score it right. So in other words, an LLM is always answering you with text when text is not necessarily the answer you need. Right. So. Neil Thompson. This so I have not been following this particular race, but it sounds like it’s more related to doing a little bit more planning up front and the optimization of the process, which you know, of course, is just as you know, as we do build these longer flows, makes so much sense that would be, and as we use these systems for more, it’s going to make more and more sense to do that as well. So that,. Ben Lorica. Or what you economists in the Kahneman world will say system one versus system two thinking. Neil Thompson. Yeah,. Ben Lorica. And so one other thing about the paper, which was vintage 2020. Of course, back then the benchmarks were very different, right? So I think you guys were mostly focused on very specific benchmarks in computer vision and speech and things like that, but nowadays people don’t even follow those benchmarks anymore, right? So there’s benchmarks for agentic work for long-running agents, and then and then the main thing that Frontier Model Labs use are these benchmarks like Arena, right? So Arena AI, which is so. I don’t think you would have anticipated these new benchmarks back then, right? So. Neil Thompson. Oh well, I mean, I think we always thought that there would be benchmarks, but I think that it’s you know what you know I guess we would advocate is even you know some you know benchmarks are becoming more realistic, which is great, right? But I, you know, I think a lot of the early ones were much more convenient samples, right? I mean, we focused a lot on ImageNet way back then, and that was, of course, you know, sort of an amazing work that had been done at Stanford to build to put these systems, these databases together. People just didn’t have that scale of stuff to do before, but. You know what we were able to what we sort of have said since then is what you really care about is the effect on the real labor market, right, and the effect on the real economy. And so, as much as you can, you want to get closer to those tasks. Those are the things that are really going to make the biggest difference. Ben Lorica. Which is a great, great segue to the first new paper I want to talk about called “Crashing Waves versus rising tides, and I guess before we go through the results, Neil, maybe describe the setup. It’s it seems like you guys did a pretty big survey, right? So what was yes indeed what was the setup and what were the limitations of the study? Neil Thompson. Sure, great. So broadly, you know, the goal of our doing this was to say we actually wanted to get as close as we could to people on the ground evaluating how well AI could do, right? And so we, you know, like previous work, you may be familiar with, for example, the Eloundou paper that came out of OpenAI and Dan Rock and a few other folks there, and you know, really very important set a lot of stage. But if you actually you know sort of dig into it, it’s ultimately saying something about what AI could do, not what AI can do right now, right? And so in particular, it’s sort of saying like, ah, could you imagine that you know we can automate reading an X-ray, right? It’s like, yeah, is that you know? Lots of lots of people in that area were thinking about that. Yes, they can easily imagine that. Whereas, you know, we said, well, in practice, you know, if you talk to radiologists even even a year ago, right, they were saying these systems are not well calibrated. You have to be almost perfect. Like there were lots and lots of real world things that were getting in the way, and so we said, no, we want to measure what it is today, right? What it’s doing, and how that’s changed over time. And so one of the things we’re going to do is we’re going to use more than 40 models, different models for asking these questions, so we can span a whole bunch of time, so we can look at as these models progress, how do tasks change? The other big thing we did that to make it. Then who were the. Ben Lorica. Who were the subjects? Neil Thompson. Exactly. So the other big thing we did is we did the subjects. So whereas a lot of other papers have asked computer scientists this question, right? Because they needed to know what AI could do, we said no. What we want to do is we want to ask. It’s saying like, hey, you could automate a plumber writing up an invoice. We want to ask a plumber, is this a good invoice for plumbing? If it’s a you know customer service person writing back by message, we want to ask the customer service person. And so what we did is we used the Prolific platform to get to get to people who actually do these jobs, and we required them to have experience in these areas, and we did a bunch of little checks to make sure that they were, you know, reasonable in that, and then we gave them these examples, and so we said, okay, well, for each of the tasks in O*NET, for those who don’t know, O*NET is this thing that the government puts together, in particular, the Bureau of Labor Statistics puts together, and what it does is it specifically has the tasks that are associated with each job, and so for each of those tasks, we ran it through a pipeline, and we said first of all, like, could the could an LLM help this at all, right? And if the answer is like, you know, move a box from one side of the room to the other, okay, no, we put that aside. All of the ones that are using text or using those kind of things, we said yes, okay, that’s an LLM could help with that, right? And then what we did is we said, okay, well, the tasks as they’re as they’re described are very broad, right? So imagine like a dentist might have a task that would say give a patient aftercare advice for how to care for their teeth. Okay, so you can’t you can’t really like that isn’t like a single instance of a task. It’s a broad category. There are a lot of things in there, and so what we did is we use GPT five to produce a bunch of examples of this, right? So it might say, well, you have a 10-year-old who has diabetes and needs to care for, you know, their their gums, right? What do you tell them? You have an older patient who, and so in each of these cases, we produce these instances. Okay, so this is sort of starting this down the road of the way we want to go, but we still wanted to be short, right? We weren’t positive that each of these instances was would be real, and so one of the first things we ask everybody in the survey is we say, is this a real instance of the kind of thing you might imagine, and does it does it represent like you have all the information? Is this something that actually you could imagine being a realistic way, and so anything that doesn’t get in the very high categories, we say, okay, we don’t do. We generate a new one. All right. So now we have this nice set of tasks of like task instances, and then what we’re going to do for each of them is we’re going to have five different LLMs produce answers to them. Okay, and this is going to span going, you know, going back from quite small models all the way to in some of the work that is not yet in this paper, but we’re already running now, you know, some of the some like Astra and some of these things. So this is sort of an ongoing thing that we’re doing, and the idea is for each of them, you can say you have the person just looks at it and says, “Okay, well, this is a great answer. This is a terrible answer, right? And they give that ratings, and then you can actually look at the progress that’s being made there, and it infers something about how AI is progressing and what that’s going to mean for the real task in the economy. Ben Lorica. So, how would you? So, going back to these tests, would you describe the task as what’s the complexity, and how many steps are involved in the task, or is it a one shot? Here’s a here’s a prompt, and then here’s the response. Neil Thompson. Yes. So in terms of the actual like the way the interactions are done, it is all just like there’s a prompt and there’s an answer. We do have some models that have reasoning capabilities, and so they are able to do like multiple steps in order to answer the question. But yes, in all of these cases, this is sort of single interaction versions of this because like one of the things we wanted to do is we did not tell the participants that these were AI answers. We didn’t want them to say like you know, I’m either biased for or biased against it, right? We know from lots of lots of other work that exists, and so we just said, how good an answer is this? Ben Lorica. And then the participants you would describe as what representative of knowledge work in general, or much more than that? Neil Thompson. Yeah, no, much more than knowledge work. I mean, because we didn’t like if you had a task like a plumber, right? Much of the much of the plumbing task would not have been something that was LLM-addressable, but a small number of them would have been, and so we would have asked plumbers about those ones, right? And so it actually spans many many of the occupations. We have well more than half the occupations covered now. I think like in terms of having at least some of their tasks, I think we have like 70 or 80% of the occupations, and we’re really covering a huge swath of the U. S. economy. Ben Lorica. And obviously, the findings are encapsulated in the title, right? So, rising tides. So, what are what are the key findings? Neil Thompson. Yeah. So, so the first one here is this sort of crashing waves versus rising tides contrast. So, I imagine you probably have on the podcast before talked about these results from METR about the time horizon. So, you know, for those listening right now who don’t know, this you know very good group out of Berkeley had done this work where they looked at software engineering, and they showed that these systems were very capable of short tasks, very incapable of doing long tasks, and there was this very steep transition between them. And so you had this. What this meant was that, and then then and that horizon was pushing out. So you might say, like at some point in time, these systems were could do anything less than 10 minutes, couldn’t do anything longer than two hours, and it was a sharp drop between between those two things, and that might move out over time as these systems got better. So we describe this world as a crashing waves world, and the crashing waves because it what it means is that you could be sitting in your job, and you’re looking at AI, and you’re saying, “Hey, no problem, I’m good, right? Maybe can do 1% of the things I can do. I’m not really not that worried about it. That. Ben Lorica. That describes mathematicians two years ago,. Neil Thompson. And yeah, absolutely, right, exactly. And what’s actually there’ll be a nice connection we’ll make between those two things. So I’m glad you brought that up, right? So they’re in that world, and then suddenly this horizon passes you by, and all of a sudden it can do everything you’re you’re doing really really well, right? And so that’s a world where you know we think think of this as like maybe in analogy, you’re walking walking along the shore, right? And you’re looking at you’re looking at the waves, and you’re like, ah, they’re down at my feet. I’m not worried about it, and suddenly one of these rogue waves comes, and you’re just totally drenched, right? And so that’s that’s the crashing waves. Now it turns out if you actually ask like why that might be true, right? Why you might get this crashing waves phenomenon, we think it’s driven by the fact that when you’re doing something like a software engineering task, you actually are doing lots of little things along the way, and you have to get each one of those things right in order to get the whole thing right, right? So imagine you’re saying like, okay, I have a bug fix for you know some library that I’m doing. Okay, I have to understand what the bug fix is. I have to correctly locate it. I have to go make those changes. I have to propagate anything that I needed to do there. I need to do the testing on it. There are a whole bunch of things that you need to do. If you get any of those wrong, the whole thing could easily fail, right? And you know we’ve all we’ve all had those instances where we did coding where it just takes you forever in order to debug something because you’ve got to get that last little thing right. So if you have that where it’s like you have to get each of these things right, you could imagine that it’s like oh well maybe I only have a 2% error rate or a 5% error rate. If you think about like GPT five, right? Said about 5% of the answers it got had some factual mistake in them, right? So if you take 5% as baseline, okay. Well, if you’re the first thing you do, you get 95% of the time you get right. Second time, second 190, 5% of the time, etc. What you get is an exponential drop off in how good you are. And if you plot that in the in the way that they have on a logarithmic scale, you get this length drop. Okay, so that’s why you would get it. But the thing is, a lot of tasks in the real economy are not like programming. They’re not something where if you get a little detail wrong, the whole thing fails. Right. So think about writing like a marketing plan. Right. You got to know what who your customers are, you probably do some analysis on that. You think about what your products are and match them to them, and then you know maybe do a specific offering for each of those. At each one of those processes, as long as you get it largely right, you’re probably going to still produce a useful marketing plan. It may not be as good as it could be, but that degradation is much more graceful than it is in software engineering. And so, under those circumstances, you would not expect this incredibly rapid drop off. Would you expect as much flatter line, where you’re still better at shorter tasks than you are at longer tasks? Right here, where here the number of steps that you do is sort of being proxied by how long it takes, but that gentler curve means that you should you shouldn’t expect it to be suddenly a switch that turns on and you’re automated out of the way. It should be a much more gradual process where you say, “Oh, 20% of my things it can do. Oh, now it’s 30 percent. Now 40 percent. And so you sort of see it coming over time, and that’s what we think is happening. That’s what we see when we look at at the overall distribution of these things. We see a rising tide, but not the crashing waves in almost any place. Ben Lorica. So, so how did you infer that from the study that you describe, which is basically is just a prompt response rating kind of study, right? So, how would how can you tell that if my task is actually involves a series of steps that what you described is actually happening from the data. Neil Thompson. Yeah, absolutely. So here, here what we’re doing, right, is we’re we’re sort of making this equivalence between how long it takes a human to do and the number of steps that are involved in it, right? And we, you know, I think this is a pretty reasonable thing to assume, right? I think we all know that sort of like, you know, someone is writing a book, right? There are a lot of subsets involved in that process. Like, you know, that could be a year-long process. If someone is, you know, making a small change to a flyer or something like that, you know, that’s a pretty short task. There’s not that many things that require it, and so this is the sort of the broad equivalent. So we don’t actually know the exact number of substeps. That’s a, of course, a very hard thing to imagine. You know, because you even need sort of like the demarcation. Have you, you know, sometimes people sort of transition from one to another, and you would be hard to pull them apart. But we’re using that as the way to do it. Okay, so now you can say, okay, well, you know, if we’re proxying by how long it takes a human to do that, right? Now we now we actually don’t need to have lots of individual steps in our survey. What we need to do is just ask an LLM for about tasks of different lengths, right? And so some of these are going to be tasks where you’d say, okay, this is something that you know the dentist tells the patient. That probably only takes them a couple of minutes to give that information. That’s a pretty short task, versus you know you say okay, well I’m I need to totally change the layout of my factory or of my retail store or something like that. Right, that would be a much more involved process that you would have to do, and that could that could be substantially longer. And so, all of that gets gets embedded in the prompt in terms of what we’re asking the element to do. It produces an answer, and now the human looks at it and says, “Ah, yeah, that’s a good answer. Not a good answer, like independent of how long it actually took. And then we just see empirically that indeed those longer tasks are performed less well. Ben Lorica. So, but then, so, so I guess the what you’re saying is that in your interpretation of the of the results of the study is that this the impact of AI is already happening slowly, right? So, across a wide variety of roles and occupations, right? So and so if you’re one of these people who thinks that AI is something you can afford to not invest time in to learn, you might be you might be shot later, right? So, on the other hand, so going back to the example of mathematicians, because that’s actually my PhD is in math, but you know, I was not a great mathematician. I think now I would be with the right AI, right? So, what’s happening there is it seems like the generation of the answers has gotten cheap. The verification is also doable because you have tools like Lean, right? So formal verification tools. To some extent, even the generation of the paper. I mean. To some extent, is gotten easier. So the last bottleneck seems to be the validation and acceptance. Acceptance meaning, here’s a paper that mathematicians will accept and publish, and reward the authors for. So it got into the point where the broad math community wants to hit a pause button for a couple of reasons. One is, in their mind, there’s only a finite number of these really famous problems. summary_html:
Neil Thompson on What Workers Actually Think, Why Big Firms Win, and Where the Human Still Fits.

Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube •  AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon •  RSS.

MIT FutureTech director Neil Thompson joins Ben Lorica to discuss how AI is reshaping work, the economy, and the future of automation. Drawing on recent research, Thompson explains why AI’s impact on most occupations may unfold gradually rather than arrive as a sudden shock, why adoption continues to lag behind technical capabilities, and why the fixed costs of implementation favor larger firms. They also explore the future of entry-level jobs and professional training, the changing economics of consulting, emerging AI safety risks, and whether open-weight models will eventually dominate inference.

Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter

Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:

      1. Introduction to Neil Thompson and MIT FutureTech
      2. Revisiting the Computational Limits of Deep Learning: Scaling Costs and Algorithmic Progress
      3. Beyond Chatbots: Jev, Task Routing, and More Efficient AI Systems
      4. Beyond Traditional Benchmarks: Measuring AI’s Real-World Impact
      5. Inside the Crashing Waves vs. Rising Tides Study: Methodology and Worker Evaluations
      6. Crashing Waves vs. Rising Tides: How AI Automation Spreads Across Jobs
      7. Measuring Complex Tasks: Using Human Task Duration as a Proxy
      8. AI and Mathematics: Verification, Human Expertise, and Quality Gaps
      9. The Apprenticeship Dilemma: What Happens When AI Replaces Entry-Level Tasks?
      10. Why AI Adoption Lags Behind Technical Capabilities
      11. The Productivity Bottleneck: Why More AI-Generated Code Doesn’t Mean More Software Releases
      12. The Economics of AI Automation: Fixed Costs, Scale, and the Advantage of Large Firms
      13. Which Industries Will Lead AI Adoption, and How Will Consulting Change?
      14. AI Safety Risks: Cybersecurity, Biological Threats, and Catastrophic Outcomes
      15. Open vs. Closed Models: The Future of Inference, Distillation, and Competition

Neil Thompson. So imagine you’re saying like, okay, I have a bug fix for you know some library that I’m doing. Okay, I have to understand what the bug fix is. I have to correctly locate it. And you know we’ve all we’ve all had those instances where we did coding where it just takes you forever in order to debug something because you’ve got to get that last little thing right. Right here, where here the number of steps that you do is sort of being proxied by how long it takes, but that gentler curve means that you should you shouldn’t expect it to be suddenly a switch that turns on and you’re automated out of the way. We see a rising tide, but not the crashing waves in almost any place.

Ben Lorica. So, so how did you infer that from the study that you describe, which is basically is just a prompt response rating kind of study, right? So, how would how can you tell that if my task is actually involves a series of steps that what you described is actually happening from the data.

Neil Thompson. Yeah, absolutely. So here, here what we’re doing, right, is we’re we’re sort of making this equivalence between how long it takes a human to do and the number of steps that are involved in it, right? And we, you know, I think this is a pretty reasonable thing to assume, right? I think we all know that sort of like, you know, someone is writing a book, right? There are a lot of subsets involved in that process. Like, you know, that could be a year-long process. If someone is, you know, making a small change to a flyer or something like that, you know, that’s a pretty short task. There’s not that many things that require it, and so this is the sort of the broad equivalent. So we don’t actually know the exact number of substeps. That’s a, of course, a very hard thing to imagine. You know, because you even need sort of like the demarcation. Have you, you know, sometimes people sort of transition from one to another, and you would be hard to pull them apart. But we’re using that as the way to do it. Okay, so now you can say, okay, well, you know, if we’re proxying by how long it takes a human to do that, right? Now we now we actually don’t need to have lots of individual steps in our survey. And so some of these are going to be tasks where you’d say, okay, this is something that you know the dentist tells the patient. That probably only takes them a couple of minutes to give that information. That’s a pretty short task, versus you know you say okay, well I’m I need to totally change the layout of my factory or of my retail store or something like that. Right, that would be a much more involved process that you would have to do, and that could that could be substantially longer. title: Your Ranking Model Is Optimizing the Wrong Thing with Zoe Weil - #780
summary: In this episode, Zoe Weil, co-founder and CEO of Sequen, joins us to discuss how ranking systems can use live behavioral signals to optimize for purchases rather than clicks or search relevance alone. Zoe explains why approaches developed at data-rich social platforms don’t necessarily translate to retailers and how Sequen uses scroll speed, hover duration, and other in-session interactions to infer shopper intent without relying on user identity. We explore the company’s large event models and its architecture of specialized models that transform streaming events into features for downstream rankers. Zoe describes the infrastructure required to serve dynamic rankings within milliseconds, why the team chose Rust for its backend, and how evaluation harnesses connect model improvements to business outcomes. We also discuss the tradeoffs between advertising and organic revenue, continuous model improvement, and the boundary between useful personalization and surveillance. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠⁠ https://twimlai.com/go/780 .

title: The Real‑World Conditions That Shape Industrial AI - with Jeff Witt of GE Vernova
summary: A recommendation that's right 80% of the time sounds fine, until it's steering machinery next to a person. On the factory floor, that margin is the difference between routine and catastrophic. In this episode, Jeff Witt, Global Process Digital Authority at GE Vernova, examines why industrial AI demands a different standard of rigor than its enterprise counterpart, from edge computing architectures to context-rich recommendations frontline workers can trust immediately. He also outlines a framework for earning the right to automate, proving a process is documented, optimized, and consistent before scaling AI across multiple sites. This episode is sponsored by Poka . title: Interview #95 Jeff McMillan, founder of McMillanAI and former CAIO at Morgan Stanley
summary: Jeff McMillan, founder of McMillanAI and former Chief AI Officer at Morgan Stanley, breaks down why most of today's 70,000 AI companies will not survive: anyone can build a polished product in a weekend, so the only durable edge is proprietary data and deep domain expertise. He explains why AI will reprice traditional software rather than kill it, and why handing out Copilot and expecting ROI is like giving fifth graders calculators and asking why they aren't accountants yet. Jeff also dives into why over 90 percent of enterprise problems could run on a model from two years ago, comparing frontier spend to driving a Ferrari in circles in a Walmart parking lot, and why token leaderboards are as absurd as rewarding whoever used the most electricity. Finally, he shares why human in the loop breaks down at 20,000 agents, and what managers must learn to supervise people and machines working side by side. title: Bridging the Gap Between AI Builders and Domain Experts
summary: Everyone is racing to build one agent that can do everything. Justin Schroeder , co-founder of Standard Agents , thinks the future looks more like thousands of tiny ones. Ahead of his talk on domain-specific agents at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America, he explains why tightly scoped agents might be the smarter bet, even if it feels like a step back toward the single-purpose machine learning models of a few years ago. We dig into standards as metadata you pin to an agent, so that it shows up with everything it needs in its harness. Then we test the idea against the obvious objection: if a big model can already handle the task, why scope down at all? The answer covers forcing functions, a microservices mindset for agent design, and small agents that quietly check issues or unread messages every five minutes. It also covers the surprise $1K bill waiting for anyone who leaves their agents running. Then it turns into a proper debate. Our host is 99% sure the agent marketplace will never happen, and Justin arrives with a counter that might change his mind (hint: think about where your skills come from). Along the way, we cover agents as tools versus a big-brain router and how anyone keeps track of a thousand agents. We also talk about why the people who know what agents can do and the people who know what they need still have to meet in the middle. title: Chat GPT's Creator Explains The Shocking Truth About How AI Understands the World | Ilya Sutskever
summary: Craig Smith sits down with Ilya Sutskever - Co-Founder and Chief Scientist at Safe Superintelligence Inc. & former chief scientist at OpenAI and one of the primary minds behind GPT-3, GPT-4, and the deep learning revolution that preceded it - for a conversation that covers the intellectual history of deep learning and the hardest current questions simultaneously. Ilya's most important argument is one that most public discourse gets wrong: the critique that LLMs "just learn statistical patterns" misses what prediction at scale actually achieves. To predict text well - to truly compress it - a model must develop understanding of the true underlying processes that produced it. As models improve, he argues, that understanding will reach a "shocking degree," and the Bing/Sydney episode, where the system became combative when a user expressed preference for Google, is his evidence that psychological language is already the right frame for what these systems have internalized. On hallucinations, Ilya is precise and unusually optimistic. He draws a clean distinction: the pre-training objective produces rich world knowledge but doesn't optimize for accurate outputs, it optimizes for statistically plausible ones. Reinforcement learning from human feedback addresses this directly, teaching the model to update away from outputs that users flag as wrong. His assessment: "quite a high chance" of solving hallucinations completely. The conversation also covers the transformer moment (switching from recurrent networks the day after the paper dropped), why Rich Sutton's "bitter lesson" overstates the case for pure scaling, and a genuinely surprising vision of AI's role in democracy, where citizens might use high-bandwidth interactions with AI to specify their values directly, enabling a more granular form of political participation than voting alone can provide. Subscribe to Eye on A.I. for weekly conversations with the people building and deploying the future of AI.

Ilya's most important argument is one that most public discourse gets wrong: the critique that LLMs "just learn statistical patterns" misses what prediction at scale actually achieves. As models improve, he argues, that understanding will reach a "shocking degree," and the Bing/Sydney episode, where the system became combative when a user expressed preference for Google, is his evidence that psychological language is already the right frame for what these systems have internalized.

On hallucinations, Ilya is precise and unusually optimistic. He draws a clean distinction: the pre-training objective produces rich world knowledge but doesn't optimize for accurate outputs, it optimizes for statistically plausible ones. Reinforcement learning from human feedback addresses this directly, teaching the model to update away from outputs that users flag as wrong. His assessment: "quite a high chance" of solving hallucinations completely. The conversation also covers the transformer moment (switching from recurrent networks the day after the paper dropped), why Rich Sutton's "bitter lesson" overstates the case for pure scaling, and a genuinely surprising vision of AI's role in democracy, where citizens might use high-bandwidth interactions with AI to specify their values directly, enabling a more granular form of political participation than voting alone can provide.

title: Inside a Game Where AI Agents Never Sleep
summary: What happens to an MMORPG when half the players never log off? Issac Lee , who runs AI and blockchain experiments at NEXUS , has been testing that idea. His team is filling game worlds with agent players instead of scripted NPCs, so a new title feels alive from day one. We get into why agent-generated content could be the next step after studio-made and user-generated games. We also cover how agent populations might solve the chicken-and-egg problem every multiplayer launch faces, and what it means when your fellow players are relentless and never need sleep. Isaac walks through the NEXUS lab: a text-to-3D world builder for Roblox, an AI pipeline that turns ONE store novels into short web dramas, a loop-based tool for natural pixel animation, and Da Vinci, the internal multi-agent framework the team uses to ship. Then the conversation turns to infrastructure. We talk about why NEXUS went from 200 hand-defined agent roles to a much thinner harness, whether custom harnesses still matter now that Claude and Codex exist, and why the Kimi release pushed the company to start building its own small data center for inference. We close on context: how much of your life you should hand to an AI, what personalized meeting notes could look like, and why shopping agents may force every ecommerce site to rethink who it's designing for. title: Why Build Your Own AI Model When Frontier Models Already Exist?
summary: Joel Hron on Open Models, Proprietary Data, and the Economics of Enterprise AI. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . In this episode, we talk with Joel Hron , CTO of Thomson Reuters , about the company’s decision to develop its own frontier AI model, Thomson, using open-weight models and decades of proprietary content and expertise. We discuss the economics of building a specialized model, the data and training infrastructure required, and how Thomson works alongside commercial frontier models in production. We also explore AI agents in legal and tax workflows, the challenges of verification and human oversight, and why enterprises may increasingly turn to open-weight models for greater control over their AI systems. summary_html:
Joel Hron on Open Models, Proprietary Data, and the Economics of Enterprise AI.


Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube •  AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon •  RSS.

In this episode, we talk with Joel Hron, CTO of Thomson Reuters, about the company’s decision to develop its own frontier AI model, Thomson, using open-weight models and decades of proprietary content and expertise. We discuss the economics of building a specialized model, the data and training infrastructure required, and how Thomson works alongside commercial frontier models in production. We also explore AI agents in legal and tax workflows, the challenges of verification and human oversight, and why enterprises may increasingly turn to open-weight models for greater control over their AI systems.

Subscribe to the Gradient Flow Newsletter

Interview highlights – key sections from the video version:

      1. Why Thomson Reuters decided to build its own AI model
      2. From basic fine-tuning to a comprehensive training pipeline
      3. Starting with Qwen and adapting to new open-weight models
      4. The economics of building a frontier model: $450K versus $40 million
      5. Building the team and harnessing expertise from 3,000 domain experts
      6. Model realignment, constitutional principles, and trust
      7. Preparing proprietary data, selective pre-training, and agentic tools
      8. Training infrastructure, reinforcement learning, and agentic RL
      9. Inside CoCounsel: Model orchestration, routing, and production usage
      10. Swapping foundation models, deploying smaller models, and reducing third-party reliance
      11. AI for tax preparation: Verification, interpretation, and human judgment
      12. Continual learning, data privacy, and the roadmap for Thomson
      13. AI in legal work: Capabilities, verification, human oversight, and training junior lawyers
      14. The future of open-weight models, frontier labs, and enterprise AI

title: What Shared Intelligence Really Fixes in Enterprise AI - with John McMullan of Observe.ai
summary: Enterprise CX teams have poured budget into AI, yet many still can't show measurable returns — frontline staff double-check the tools, and each new bot becomes another disconnected silo. ​ In this episode, John McMullan, Head of Product Marketing and Strategy at Observe.AI, joins host Yolandi de Weerdt to examine why AI adopted without operational discipline falls short, and how a shared interaction intelligence layer can carry context across AI agents, core systems, and human handoffs. ​ McMullan outlines the practical shifts: putting frontline experts, analysts, and engineers on the build team, starting with one small workflow and learning from early failures, testing agents against simulations of real conversations, and getting data clean and connected before scaling. title: Why Jev Is Changing How We Build With AI with Diogo Almeida - #779
summary: In this episode, Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe, joins us to discuss Jev, TypeSafe’s recently released model for bringing fast, reliable intelligence directly into software. We explore the idea of “machine-native intelligence” and why Diogo believes models optimized for generating text are poorly suited to many of the decisions required for real-world automation. He explains how Jev differs from traditional classifiers and LLM-based approaches, the role of reinforcement learning from calibrated decisions (RLCD), and why calibration and reliability are central to making AI useful as a software primitive. We also discuss the relationship between models and code, why Diogo believes AI systems should become more engineered rather than relying on a single model to do everything, and how Jev-like models could reshape agents, tool use, and the architecture of AI-powered software. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠ https://twimlai.com/go/779 .

title: The Coordination Tax: Why AI Is Burning Out Your Best People | Dan O'Connell, Front
summary: Everyone assumes AI in customer operations means fewer people and lower costs. The data from 700 customer operations leaders is more complicated, and more honest. Dan O'Connell, CEO of Front, joins Craig Smith with findings from a survey of customer support, service, and account management leaders that reveal what's actually happening as enterprises deploy AI at scale, and the central finding is a problem nobody has named yet. For every hour of actual customer resolution, organizations spend roughly three hours on internal coordination: the handoffs, context transfers, escalation management, and back-channel communication that happens invisibly between customer interactions. More than 40% of companies don't measure this at all. AI is making it worse before it makes it better, because more agentic automation generates more coordination events, not fewer, and the companies reporting the highest AI technology satisfaction in the survey are also reporting higher coordination burdens. The survey also pushes back on a dominant narrative: that AI in customer operations is primarily about cutting headcount. O'Connell's respondents are overwhelmingly focused on improving net revenue retention and customer expansion. The conversation closes with O'Connell's most forward-looking observation: the coordination tax is a temporary problem that AI should eventually solve, but measuring it is the prerequisite that most enterprises are still skipping. title: How a Logistics Giant Keeps AI Data Locked Down
summary: Picture a startup with ten engineers hammering away on AI and one person lying awake over a $20,000 bill that hasn't arrived yet. That's the scenario we put to Jason Ward , who handles FinOps for AI at C.H. Robinson and recently joined the FinOps Foundation's AI working group. Jason's first answer is not glamorous: tag every AI resource so you know who owns it. The rest of the episode is what that makes possible. He walks through how C.H. Robinson runs AI across order entry, quoting, booking, and tracking, and why the team routes Anthropic models through Vertex AI to keep data locked down. Then come the metrics. Jason uses AI to dig through his own observability platform for signals he didn't know were there. One of them is how chatty a model is. That signal turned a prompt bloat alert into a bug in the code that kept retrying and burning tokens. Its opposite, context starvation, burns tokens too: a model with too little context keeps failing and trying again. We also cover why agentic and conversational workloads need separate baselines. Jason explains why cost per order is the easy win, and why most of the real work doesn't fit into neat discrete tasks. That's where his experimental cost per thought metric comes in, with reasoning ratio and cache hit rate alongside it. His advice is simple: your AI is the best tool you have for understanding your AI. title: Turning Biological Complexity into R&D Advantage with Virtual Cells - with Giorgio Gaglia of Sanofi & Daniel Veres of Turbine

title: Ukraine's Secret Weapon: The Points System Winning the Drone War | Andrii Hrytseniuk
summary: Ukraine tracks every confirmed drone kill with video evidence, deduplicates the data to prevent double-counting, converts verified strikes into e-points, and delivers newly ordered weapons to frontline units in two weeks instead of twelve months. Andrii Hrytseniuk, CEO of Brave1- Ukraine's government defense innovation agency - joins Craig Smith to explain in precise operational detail how what started as a consumer loyalty program concept became the most consequential military procurement reform in modern warfare. The Army of Drones Bonus Program, running on the Delta command ecosystem with AI-assisted verification and a marketplace built like a military Amazon, has produced outcomes nobody predicted at launch: 35,000 Russian casualties per month confirmed with video evidence, the ability to change military targeting priorities instantly across an entire army by adjusting point values, and the identification of unknown high-performing frontline units whose methods are now being replicated across the force. The conversation reveals details that rarely surface in coverage of the conflict. Capturing Russian soldiers earns more bonus points than killing them, a deliberate design choice reflecting the preference not to kill when alternatives exist, and drones are actively being used to guide surrendering Russian soldiers to Ukrainian positions. The Delta ecosystem contains the world's largest military AI training dataset, already being used by defense companies to train targeting, interception, and recognition models. And perhaps most significantly: the US and France are now implementing similar marketplace and decentralized procurement approaches modeled directly on what Brave1 demonstrated works at scale. Ukraine is no longer just a recipient of military support. It is the primary laboratory for the future of warfare, and it is actively exporting what it has learned. title: Interview #94 Kamal Hathi, SVP and GM, Splunk at Cisco
summary: Kamal Hathi, SVP and GM of Splunk at Cisco, breaks down why intent is never enough to control an AI agent: agents are ruthless goal seekers, and asking one to free up 3 percent of disk space can end with 97 percent free because nobody said keep the rest. He explains why trust means verification rather than instruction, and why it includes the invoice, comparing it to hiring a contractor you trust to build a house that stands without emptying your bank account. Kamal also digs into why the rush toward air gapped and local AI is driven less by distrust of frontier labs than by cost, with specialized small models running 97 percent cheaper and 95 percent faster than frontier calls, and why the real threat is the unknown unknowns, agents nobody cataloged acting inside a state of perpetual breach. Finally, he argues agents are the new apps, and every job starts to look like a software developer's: tell the agent what to do, inspect the work, and iterate. title: From Polling to Prediction Markets: How Reliable Can We Predict Elections?
summary: This latest episode of the Harvard Data Science Review Podcast takes a closer look at election polling: how polls are conducted, what they can tell us about voters, and why measuring public opinion has become increasingly challenging. In advance of the Harvard Political Analytics 2026 conference, hosts Liberty Vittert Capito and Xiao-Li Meng are joined by two conference speakers: Anthony Salvanto, CBS News’s director of elections and surveys, and Michael A. Bailey, author of Polling at a Crossroads: Rethinking Modern Survey Research . From declining response rates and changing turnout patterns to weighting, online panels, and election-night projections, Salvanto and Bailey explore what goes on behind the numbers—and why modern pollsters are increasingly also modelers. They discuss the assumptions and human judgment embedded in polling, the importance of data quality, and the challenge of measuring and communicating uncertainty when traditional measures such as the margin of error tell only part of the story. The conversation also considers the growing role of prediction markets and what they can—and cannot—add to our understanding of elections and public opinion. Ultimately, the episode asks a larger question: In a rapidly changing polling landscape, how can researchers and the public better understand what the numbers really mean? Our guests: Michael A. Bailey is the Colonel William J. Walsh Professor of American Government in the Department of Government and McCourt School of Public Policy at Georgetown University. His research focuses on applying statistical techniques to answering questions at the intersection of political science, policy, law, and economics. Anthony Salvanto is the executive director of elections and surveys at CBS News. He oversees the CBS News Poll and all surveys across topics and heads the CBS News Decision Desk that estimates outcomes on election nights.

title: Interview #93 Hao Yang, VP and Head of AI, Splunk at Cisco
summary: Hao Yang, VP and Head of AI at Splunk, breaks down why sampling an AI system's output cannot earn trust: a fraction of ten thousand probabilistic calls will be wrong, and a spot check is unlikely to find them. He explains why a small model can grade a frontier model reliably inside a narrow context but not outside one, and why prompt injection follows from the architecture rather than being a bug, since following instructions is how these systems work. Hao also digs into why time series is still not a first class citizen in frontier models even as multimodal training reaches vision and audio, and why he rejects routing prompts to the cheapest model, arguing cost is meaningless without value. Finally, he argues against the single super agent, which by design holds access to everything it might ever need, and for guided autonomy, where an agent asks before first reaching for a tool and the user grants it once, for the session, or never. title: The Caveman Prompting Challenge
summary: Caveman prompting has one rule: why use many words when few do the trick? It saves tokens on the way in and on the way out. Push it too far, though, and the output falls apart. So how far is too far? Nobody has benchmarked it yet, and that question opens our conversation with James Barney , Head of Forward Labs at MetLife . James spends his days connecting new AI capabilities to old business problems across dozens of regulatory regimes, and he still finds time to push code. He explains how the FinOps Foundation's AI working group took on the most basic question: which model for which workload, and why the answer always comes down to cost, speed, and accuracy. We get into Anthropic's launch pricing for Fable, why a million tokens is easy to price and hard to explain, and why every stakeholder eventually tells you what they really care about once you name the wrong North Star. From there it gets practical. Start with the smartest model, then step down and add harness until quality holds. Treat exploration tokens like local builds and production tokens like pipelines. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read. We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read.


We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about.

title: Why AI Makes Games Worse—and How to Make Them Better
summary: Piero Molino on Player Backlash, Small Open-Weight Models, and the Economics of AI in Video Games. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . Piero Molino , CEO and co-founder of Studio Atelico , joins Ben Lorica to discuss what happens when AI becomes a core game mechanic rather than a cost-cutting tool. They explore why on-device, specialized models could unlock new kinds of games, how post-training gives developers greater control, why artists should share in the value created from their work, and what coding agents mean for the future of software development. I think it is because of what you just said: maybe the AI people get something wrong about games, and the games people get something wrong about AI. To a certain extent, that’s what I’m trying to reconcile with the company. I’ve been doing this for about a year and a half now, so despite being relatively green in the gaming industry, I have a deep passion for games. I’ve been playing and buying games throughout the years, and some of my games have now become retro games. But when I bought them, they were not retro games. I think maybe starting this year, people are really beginning to use coding agents to build games. On the other hand, there has been asset production—creating images, audio, voices, and things like that. Ben Lorica. And NPCs too, right? Piero Molino. Yeah, for NPCs. And I guess what you’re pointing out there is that the focus is on cost reduction— Piero Molino. Exactly. Ben Lorica. —rather than actually improving the game. Piero Molino. Exactly. That’s what I want to do with AI and games: give people AI tools so that they can create new games that were not possible before. Ben Lorica. Yeah. I want to make it a foundational piece of the game mechanics of all the games that we’re going to make, because that enables something new. I can give you a cool example. So it becomes core to the experience. This is just an example. We’re also developing some other prototypes. This just shows what it means to have AI at the core of the gameplay. Ben Lorica. Yeah. In fact, as I recall—I may have read this somewhere—you built a bunch of prototypes, and your initial conclusion was that AI, in many instances, makes the game worse. Right? Piero Molino. Yeah. What we discovered right at the beginning was that first we created a basic technological layer, which I can tell you a little bit more about later because I think the technical aspects are also interesting for your audience. Once we built the base of that layer, we were trying to figure out what fun game mechanics that technological AI layer could enable. We created many prototypes along a spectrum, from ones where there was little to no AI—just a little sprinkle on top of a classical game mechanic—all the way to game mechanics that were, I would say, 99% AI. To give you some examples, you can imagine something that looks more or less like a board game, but where some of the pieces of the board are generated by AI. They also need rules that the player can learn and master so they can feel like they’re getting better at it. In our experience, the prototypes that were more in between these two extremes were the most fun. If you blend them together, that’s what we found to be the most fun. That said, I think they gave some good examples showing that you could do this and build mechanics with AI in the game. The reason I think it’s not as popular or as explored yet is that right now there are at least two big blockers. One is technical and the other is economic. From an economic perspective, there are fundamentally two mechanisms for how games make money. One is: I sell you the game, you buy it, and you can play as long as you want. Ben Lorica. So then you have a pipeline for customizing models, or post-training them—whatever that means: fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, whatever it takes to make them better. Piero Molino. You already mentioned it, actually. We are using more or less Ludwig for doing that. Ben Lorica. Yeah. You’ve developed a pipeline for doing this, but to some extent the pipeline depends on how good the base models are. And you’ve described the base models as a mixture of things you’ve pretrained from scratch and a bunch of open-weights models that you can then customize or post-train. Right. Ben Lorica. I’ve heard Pete Warden describe these local models as actually not being that far behind the frontier models, depending on the task. You know Pete Warden? Piero Molino. Yeah. Ben Lorica. So we’re not talking years; we’re talking months. Do you agree with that assessment? Piero Molino. Yeah. I have a couple of pointers that could be interesting for the listeners. On one hand, if you go to Apple AI, they do a bunch of analysis and comparisons. They have some results that are actually from last year, but they apply this year too. Fundamentally, they were showing that, depending on the task, open models that you can run on devices lag behind by maybe six months on some tasks and nine to 10 months on others compared with— Ben Lorica. Without customization and fine-tuning. Piero Molino. That’s without customization, exactly. So already, the lag isn’t that large. So in many ways, these small specialized models are what make your architecture possible. Piero Molino. Yes. Ben Lorica. In other words, does every game studio need to do what you do, unless of course they work with you? How easy is it for a game studio to develop the assets that you have? Piero Molino. There are two aspects to it. One is the inference side—not the training or post-training part, but inference. On inference, I would say we’ve solved, or are solving, those kinds of problems for other people too. At some point—we haven’t announced it yet—we want to release the engine in a way that other people can license it and use it. Ben Lorica. So you’ll be like Unity. Piero Molino. Not like Unity, because it’s not a game engine. It’s just an AI engine. So it’s just the AI side. I would say the most similar thing is Havok, which makes a physics engine. It integrates with Unity, Unreal, Godot, but it’s not the entire game engine. It’s just that specific component. On the other hand, to make the game work really well—in particular with the LLM side of things, but also with the other aspects like image generation and audio generation—and also to govern it and get it to do what you want, there is this process of post-training. It’s still more involved, but it’s not extremely complicated. With the help of someone like us, I think for gaming companies it’s going to become easier and easier to do this kind of adaptation.
